course.title: React: Components, State and Effects
course.subtitle: Build reusable, accessible React interfaces with predictable state and disciplined side effects.
course.description: A practical React course covering component composition, JSX, props, list keys, state snapshots, events, controlled forms, conditional and derived UI, Effects as external synchronization, dependencies and cleanup, context, custom Hooks, asynchronous data, accessibility, component testing and server/client rendering boundaries. Learners build a tested course catalogue.
target_audience: Developers preparing for modern React and Next.js work
prerequisites: Basic TypeScript knowledge is helpful but not required
outcomes: Break an interface into cohesive reusable components
Use JSX, props and stable list keys correctly
Model state updates as immutable snapshots
Handle events and controlled forms accessibly
Derive UI from minimal state rather than duplicate values
Use Effects only to synchronize with external systems
Share state through context and custom Hooks appropriately
Test async, accessible React user journeys
course.accessibility: Components use semantic HTML, labels and keyboard-operable controls. Examples include focus, error and loading states. All diagrams have text descriptions.

sections.title: React Components and Declarative UI
sections.description: Describe interfaces with reusable components, JSX and props.

lessons.title: What React is and how components compose
lessons.body_markdown:
## What React is and how components compose

React is a library for describing user interfaces as reusable components. A component receives inputs and returns a description of what should appear. Components can be nested to form a tree, allowing a page to be divided into cohesive units such as a navigation bar, course card and progress panel. A component should be predictable from its props and state. Avoid designing components as miniature pages with unrelated responsibilities. Composition lets a parent choose which children to render without forcing every component into a rigid inheritance hierarchy.

### Worked example

Sketch a course dashboard tree containing a header, catalogue list, course card and progress summary. Identify which parts should be separate components.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not create a component for every wrapper element; components should have a meaningful responsibility or reuse boundary.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Break a page into components and explain the data each child needs.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind what react is and how components compose.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: JSX and rendering values
lessons.body_markdown:
## JSX and rendering values

JSX is a syntax extension that lets components describe UI using markup-like expressions. It compiles to JavaScript calls and is not HTML text inserted directly into the source file. JavaScript expressions can be embedded with braces, while statements such as `if` need to be expressed through surrounding JavaScript logic or conditional rendering patterns. Text and attributes should be treated as values; rendering untrusted content as raw HTML needs special care. Keep rendering logic readable and avoid deeply nested conditional expressions.

### Worked example

Create JSX for a course card using a title expression, a level label and a conditional badge.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not assume JSX is a string template or insert untrusted HTML without an explicit sanitisation strategy.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Translate a data object into a JSX component and identify expressions versus markup.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind jsx and rendering values.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Props, composition and component contracts
lessons.body_markdown:
## Props, composition and component contracts

Props are inputs passed from a parent to a child component. They should be treated as read-only by the receiving component. A well-designed component has a small, clear prop contract with meaningful names and appropriate types. Composition through children or named slots can make a component flexible without adding dozens of Boolean flags. Avoid copying props into state unless there is a deliberate reason to manage a separate editable value. Stable component contracts make reuse and testing easier.

### Worked example

Create a `CourseCard` component that receives a course object and an optional action area through children.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not mutate props or create duplicated state that can drift away from the source value.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Write a prop contract for a reusable course card and identify which values belong to the parent.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind props, composition and component contracts.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Rendering lists and keys
lessons.body_markdown:
## Rendering lists and keys

React renders collections by mapping data into elements. Each sibling in a list needs a stable key that helps React match items across updates. A database identifier is usually better than an array index when records can be reordered, inserted or deleted. Keys are not passed to the child as ordinary props. Missing or unstable keys can produce incorrect state association and warnings. Avoid using random values as keys during rendering because they force unnecessary remounting.

### Worked example

Render a course list using stable course IDs and test what happens when one item is inserted at the beginning.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not use an array index as a key for a list whose ordering or membership can change.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Explain why stable keys matter when a learner's course list is sorted or filtered.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind rendering lists and keys.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

sections.title: State, Events and Rendering
sections.description: Model interface state and handle user interaction predictably.

lessons.title: State as a snapshot
lessons.body_markdown:
## State as a snapshot

React state belongs to a component instance and each render receives a snapshot of that state. Calling a setter schedules a future render; it does not change the state variable inside the already-running handler. When a new state depends on the previous state, use the updater function form to avoid stale values. State should be treated as immutable: create a new object or array rather than mutating the existing one. These rules help React detect changes and keep event behaviour predictable.

### Worked example

Create a counter with increment and reset actions, then update an array of selected course IDs without mutating it.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not expect reading a state variable immediately after calling its setter to return the updated value.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Trace two state updates in one event and explain why an updater function may be necessary.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind state as a snapshot.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Events and user interaction
lessons.body_markdown:
## Events and user interaction

React event handlers are functions passed to JSX elements. They run in response to user interactions such as clicks, form input and keyboard activation. Keep handlers focused on a user action and move complex logic into named functions when helpful. Event propagation follows familiar browser concepts, but React's event system has its own implementation details. Use semantic buttons, links and form controls so keyboard and assistive-technology behaviour are available by default. A visible control must perform the action its label promises.

### Worked example

Build an enrolment button with a handler that updates local status and prevents duplicate submissions while pending.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not attach interactive behaviour to a generic `div` when a native button or link expresses the action.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Test an interaction with pointer and keyboard and verify the control's disabled/loading state.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind events and user interaction.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Controlled forms and validation
lessons.body_markdown:
## Controlled forms and validation

A controlled input receives its current value from React state and updates that state through an event handler. This allows a component to display validation feedback and keep the visible value consistent with application state. For larger forms, group related state and validate at clear boundaries. Client-side validation improves feedback but the server remains responsible for checking input and permissions. Associate errors with fields and preserve user-entered values when submission fails. Avoid making the UI state more complicated than the form's actual rules require.

### Worked example

Build a controlled course-search input and a form that reports a missing course selection.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not treat React state as a security boundary or assume a controlled input guarantees valid submitted data.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Write tests for empty, valid and malformed form values and verify the error appears beside the correct field.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind controlled forms and validation.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Conditional rendering and derived values
lessons.body_markdown:
## Conditional rendering and derived values

React can render different UI based on state and props using conditions, early returns and logical expressions. Derived values should usually be calculated from existing props and state instead of stored separately. Duplicate state creates synchronization problems: when one value changes, every copied value must also be updated. Use memoization only when a measured performance need or stable reference requirement justifies it. Conditional branches should cover loading, empty, success and failure states explicitly.

### Worked example

Render a course list with separate loading, empty and populated views derived from one data state.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not store a filtered list in separate state when it can be derived from the source list and active filter.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Model a search result panel using a minimal state shape and derive its visible list.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind conditional rendering and derived values.

sections.title: Effects, Context and Reusable Logic
sections.description: Synchronize with external systems and share state responsibly.

lessons.title: Effects as synchronization with external systems
lessons.body_markdown:
## Effects as synchronization with external systems

An Effect synchronizes a component with an external system after rendering. Examples include subscribing to an event source, controlling a non-React widget or connecting to a browser API. Effects are not a general-purpose place to calculate derived values or respond to every user action; those tasks often belong in render logic or event handlers. The dependency list describes the reactive values used by the Effect, and cleanup reverses the setup when the dependency changes or component unmounts. Keep the external synchronization boundary explicit.

### Worked example

Subscribe to a browser event in an Effect and remove the listener in its cleanup function.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not use an Effect to copy one state variable into another when a derived calculation can solve the problem.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Identify which parts of a component need an Effect and which belong in render or an event handler.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind effects as synchronization with external systems.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Effect dependencies and cleanup
lessons.body_markdown:
## Effect dependencies and cleanup

Effect dependencies must include the reactive values used by the Effect so that synchronization stays correct as values change. Omitting a dependency can create stale closures; adding unstable dependencies can cause repeated setup. A cleanup function runs before the Effect re-synchronizes and when the component unmounts. Development Strict Mode may intentionally run setup and cleanup more than once to reveal unsafe assumptions. Write Effects so setup and cleanup form a repeatable pair, and avoid suppressing lint rules without understanding the dependency model.

### Worked example

Create an Effect that starts a timer using a stable callback and clears it whenever the relevant configuration changes.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not hide a missing dependency warning by disabling the lint rule; determine why the effect needs the value.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Trace setup, cleanup and re-setup when a prop changes.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind effect dependencies and cleanup.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Context and state sharing
lessons.body_markdown:
## Context and state sharing

Context lets a component read a value provided by an ancestor without passing it through every intermediate component. It is useful for cross-cutting values such as theme, locale or an authenticated user's display context. Context does not replace all state management, and frequent broad context changes can cause many consumers to rerender. Keep providers as close as practical to the components that need them and separate unrelated contexts. For complex domain state, a reducer or dedicated state layer may be clearer.

### Worked example

Create a theme context for a course dashboard and keep course filter state local to the catalogue.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not put every application value into one global context simply to avoid passing props.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Choose which values belong in local state, lifted state or context and explain why.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind context and state sharing.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Custom Hooks and reusable behaviour
lessons.body_markdown:
## Custom Hooks and reusable behaviour

A custom Hook is a function whose name begins with `use` and that can call React Hooks at its top level. It packages reusable stateful behaviour, such as tracking online status or managing a form, without creating a new component layer. Hooks must be called in the same order on every render and not inside conditions or loops. A custom Hook should return a small useful interface and avoid hiding too much behaviour behind vague names. Reuse should simplify the caller rather than create an abstraction that is harder to understand.

### Worked example

Create a `useOnlineStatus` Hook that subscribes to browser online/offline events and cleans up its listeners.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not call a Hook conditionally or from an ordinary utility function.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Write a custom Hook contract and list the state and actions exposed to its caller.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind custom hooks and reusable behaviour.

sections.title: Testing and Production-Ready React
sections.description: Build accessible, tested components and integrate asynchronous data.

lessons.title: Asynchronous data and loading states
lessons.body_markdown:
## Asynchronous data and loading states

A component that loads data must represent the request lifecycle: pending, success, empty and failure. Starting requests in Effects can be appropriate for client-only synchronization, but framework data-loading patterns or dedicated query libraries may be better for caching, deduplication and server rendering. Cancel obsolete requests or ignore stale responses when parameters change. Preserve clear loading semantics and do not show old data as fresh after a failed request. Every asynchronous operation needs a defined error path.

### Worked example

Load a list of courses with an Effect, cancel or disregard obsolete requests and display a retry action on failure.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not assume a fetch Promise rejects on an HTTP 404; inspect the Response status and handle it.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Test delayed success, empty results, HTTP failure and a request that becomes obsolete.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind asynchronous data and loading states.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Accessibility and component testing
lessons.body_markdown:
## Accessibility and component testing

Accessible React components use semantic HTML, labels, headings, focus management and clear status messages. Automated tests should query elements the way users perceive them, using roles and accessible names where practical. Test observable behaviour rather than component internals. Include keyboard interaction, form errors and loading/disabled states. A snapshot test alone rarely proves that a workflow is usable. Keep test data realistic and avoid depending on production accounts or network services for routine component tests.

### Worked example

Write a component test that submits an enrolment form and checks the accessible error message and success status.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not test only internal state setters when the user's actual interaction and displayed outcome matter.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Create a test matrix for a course card, search form and enrolment button.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind accessibility and component testing.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Server and client rendering boundaries
lessons.body_markdown:
## Server and client rendering boundaries

React can participate in different rendering environments. Traditional client-rendered components execute in the browser, while server-rendered or framework-managed components may produce HTML before browser hydration. Browser-only APIs cannot be accessed during server rendering unless guarded or moved into a client-side boundary. Hydration expects the initial client render to match the server-rendered HTML; reading unstable values such as the current time during the initial render can create mismatches. Frameworks such as Next.js define explicit server/client component patterns beyond core React.

### Worked example

Explain why accessing `window.localStorage` during a server render can fail and show where browser-only work belongs.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not assume every React component runs only in the browser when using a server-rendering framework.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Identify server-safe and browser-only operations in a sample component tree.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind server and client rendering boundaries.
Identify one state, accessibility, rendering or effect-lifecycle condition that must be tested.

lessons.title: Build a complete React application
lessons.body_markdown:
## Build a complete React application

A well-structured React application uses components for cohesive UI units, state for values that change, derived calculations for values that can be recomputed, and Effects only for external synchronization. Define data contracts and request states before wiring a service. Use semantic controls, stable keys and testable boundaries. Keep asynchronous failures visible and check the application at mobile widths and with keyboard navigation. A project is not complete because the first route renders; test the main user journey and document remaining gaps.

### Worked example

Build a course catalogue with filters, detail views, enrolment state, request loading/error handling and responsive components.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not bury all state and data logic inside one page component or use Effects as a substitute for a clear event flow.

### Check your understanding

Explain the component's inputs, state and visible result. Identify whether the behaviour belongs in rendering, an event handler or an Effect, and describe how cleanup, loading and error states are handled. Keep the user's observable behaviour as the test target.
lessons.exercise: Submit a working React application with component tests, keyboard review and a short architecture note.
key_takeaways: Explain the React concept behind build a complete react application.

assessment.title: React: Components, State and Effects Final Assessment
assessment.instructions: Answer all questions with component and lifecycle reasoning. Code should use stable keys, clear state contracts and tested user-visible behaviour.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between props and state, and why a child component should not mutate its props.
Design the minimal state for a course catalogue with a search term, selected level and request lifecycle. Identify values that should be derived.
A component uses an Effect to copy a filtered array into state whenever the source array changes. Explain why this is unnecessary and propose a derived render calculation.
An Effect adds an event listener but never removes it. Explain the lifecycle defect and provide a cleanup strategy.
Design tests for an enrolment form using keyboard interaction, labelled errors, pending state and successful submission.
Submit the course catalogue application with source, tests and architecture note.

final_project.title: React Course Catalogue
final_project.brief: Build a catalogue where learners can search and filter courses, open a detail view and begin a simulated enrolment. Use reusable components, minimal state, derived filtering and stable keys. Handle asynchronous data with explicit loading, empty and error states. Use Effects only for external synchronization such as subscriptions or request lifecycle where appropriate. Include accessible forms and component tests.
deliverables: At least 10 component or utility tests
README with setup and run instructions
acceptance_criteria: Search and filters produce correct results
State updates do not mutate existing objects or arrays
Form and buttons are keyboard accessible
Errors and pending states are visible
